messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The first time Elias Vance realized his body could turn against him, he was seventeen, gasping on the floor of his university dorm. The collapse had been sudden, a violent cascade of symptoms that landed him in the emergency department and later the intensive care unit. For three weeks, his reality was defined by the sharp, repeated pinch of blood draws, the cold bite of a venous drip threading into his arm, and the invasive glare of a scope passing down his throat. Through it all, the air remained thick with the sterile, iodine-heavy scent of the hospital wards. He survived the illness, but the months of recovery left a lasting fracture, and when he finally returned to campus, the physical architecture of his daily life had permanently shifted. At first, the triggers were sporadic but relentless. The sharp sight of a needle on a campus nurse’s tray immediately sparked a hot rush of panic, his palms sweating and his chest tightening as if he were back on that gurney. When his body flared into that familiar state of physical reactivity, a quieter conviction began to take root. He started to feel that he could no longer trust his own physiology, that it had already proven itself capable of sudden betrayal. The moment a medical procedure was mentioned or an examination table came into view, that terror drove him to avoid hospitals, ambulances, and any clinic where his body might be inspected. He found himself skipping counseling practicum sessions that discussed trauma narratives, convinced that listening to those topics would only feed the fire. His conviction that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore pushed him further into withdrawal, which in turn taught him to delay sleep, staying up until his eyes burned just to keep his guard up. Fearing that his own body was an enemy waiting to react, he began scanning every room for physical cues, which only magnified the potency of the hospital antiseptic smell drifting from nearby wellness centers. The constant physical reactivity left him chronically drained, which meant he had to push himself away from medical cues even harder and continue delaying sleep to avoid the vulnerability of lying down. His refusal to rest stripped his nervous system of recovery, so the threat of a sudden startle to movement worsened; a dropped textbook or his roommate’s sudden gesture now jolted him into a full-body flinch. That lingering physical tension kept his nerves wound tight, so the mere whir of a refrigerator or a glint of metal triggered the same visceral dread, pulling him back into the cycle. By his junior year, the loop was tightening. He worked as a peer counselor at the university health center, a role that now felt like walking through a minefield. He had to leave a session when a student’s IV arm came into view, his vision blurring with the old terror, and his exhaustion from sleepless nights made him flinch at his girlfriend Lena’s sudden touches, creating a quiet, aching distance between them. Now, at nineteen, Elias sits in the office of a community clinic, his palms damp on the folder in his lap. The PCL5 assessment that landed him here reflects a score that feels less like a number and more like a full-body confession. He came because the sleepless nights have given way to daytime dizziness, and because he is terrified that the cycle will leave him completely isolated. What he hopes for, more than anything, is to stop waiting for his body to fail him again, and to find a way back to the life he thought he was building.
